reminder: An integrable system has differential equations that one can solve in closed form or by integrals.
definition: An integrable system is a system of [differential equations](c:differential-equation), often a Hamiltonian system, that one can solve in closed form or by quadratures, that is, by finitely many integrals. There is no single formal definition; the most common precise one is a [Liouville integrable system](c:liouville-integrable-system), which has as many independent conserved quantities with zero [Poisson bracket](c:poisson-bracket) as degrees of freedom.
examples: The harmonic oscillator and the two-body Kepler problem have enough conserved quantities to solve the motion by quadratures.
The Korteweg-de Vries equation is an infinite-dimensional system with infinitely many conserved quantities.
Non-example: the planar double pendulum has chaotic orbits and no complete set of independent conserved quantities, so it is not integrable.

steps: Take a Liouville integrable system, a Hamiltonian system with $n$ degrees of freedom and $n$ independent conserved quantities in involution.
Liouville's theorem then solves its equations by quadratures.
So the system is solvable in closed form, and it is integrable in the broad sense.
The broad notion also covers systems with infinitely many degrees of freedom, such as the KdV equation.
links.why: A result about integrable systems applies to every Liouville integrable system, the best understood case.

reminder: An integral equation is an equation in which the unknown function appears under an integral sign.
definition: An integral equation is an [equation](c:equation) for an unknown [function](c:function) $\varphi$ in which $\varphi$ appears under an [integral](c:integral) sign. A typical linear form is $\varphi(x)=f(x)+\lambda\int_a^bK(x,t)\,\varphi(t)\,dt$, where $K$ is a given [integral kernel](c:integral-kernel) and $f$ is a given function; it is a Volterra equation when the upper limit is $x$ and a Fredholm equation when both limits are fixed.
examples: The equation $\varphi(x)=1+\tfrac12\int_0^1xt\,\varphi(t)\,dt$ is a Fredholm equation with the solution $\varphi(x)=1+\tfrac{3}{10}x$.
The Volterra equation $\varphi(x)=1+\int_0^x\varphi(t)\,dt$ has the solution $\varphi(x)=e^x$.
Non-example: $\varphi'(x)=\varphi(x)$ is a differential equation, because the unknown appears only through its derivative and not under an integral sign.

reminder: An integral kernel is a function of two variables that turns a function into a new function by integration.
definition: Let $(X,\mu)$ and $(Y,\nu)$ be [measure spaces](c:measure-space). An integral kernel is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $K:X\times Y\to\mathbb C$ that is used to send a function $f$ on $Y$ to the function $x\mapsto\int_YK(x,y)f(y)\,d\nu(y)$ on $X$, where the integral is a [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral).
examples: The Fourier kernel $K(x,y)=e^{-ixy}$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ gives the Fourier transform.
The Poisson kernel gives the harmonic extension of boundary values on the unit disc.
Non-example: the identity map on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ has no kernel function $K$, because only the Dirac distribution $\delta(x-y)$ plays that role, and it is not a function.

steps: Take open sets $X,Y\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a locally integrable kernel function $K$ on $X\times Y$.
The kernel defines the operator $T_K\psi(x)=\int K(x,y)\psi(y)\,dy$ from test functions on $Y$ to functions on $X$.
Its Schwartz kernel is the distribution $\varphi\otimes\psi\mapsto\int_X\varphi\,T_K\psi$, and this distribution is given by the function $K$.
A general Schwartz kernel may be a distribution such as $\delta(x-y)$ that is not a function.
links.why: Statements about Schwartz kernels apply to every operator that an integral kernel defines.

reminder: An integral operator sends a function $f$ to the function $x\mapsto\int K(x,y)f(y)\,dy$ for a fixed kernel $K$.
definition: Given an [integral kernel](c:integral-kernel) $K$, the integral operator $T_K$ is the [linear map](c:linear-map) $(T_Kf)(x)=\int K(x,y)f(y)\,dy$ on the [functions](c:function) $f$ for which the integral exists. Common cases are $T_K:L^2\to L^2$ with $K$ square integrable, and Volterra operators with $K(x,y)=0$ for $y>x$.
examples: The Volterra operator $(Vf)(x)=\int_0^xf(t)\,dt$ has the kernel $K(x,t)=1$ for $t\le x$ and $K(x,t)=0$ otherwise.
The Fourier transform and convolution with a function $g$ are integral operators, with kernels $e^{-ixy}$ and $g(x-y)$.
Non-example: differentiation $f\mapsto f'$ is not an integral operator, because no function $K(x,y)$ gives $\int K(x,y)f(y)\,dy=f'(x)$ for all test functions $f$.

steps: Take an integral operator $T_K$, functions $f,g$ and scalars $a,b$.
The integral is linear, so $\int K(x,y)(af+bg)(y)\,dy=a\,(T_Kf)(x)+b\,(T_Kg)(x)$.
So $T_K$ is a linear map.
The special case adds that the map is an integration against a kernel.
links.why: Facts about linear maps apply to every integral operator.

steps: Take a Hilbert-Schmidt operator $T$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$.
It is given by a kernel $K\in L^2(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n)$ through $(Tf)(x)=\int K(x,y)f(y)\,dy$.
So $T$ is an integral operator.
The Hilbert-Schmidt case adds that the kernel is square integrable.
links.why: A result for integral operators applies to every Hilbert-Schmidt operator on an $L^2$ space.

reminder: The interchange law says that horizontal and vertical composition of 2-cells give the same result in either order.
definition: In a [2-category](c:2-category), let $\alpha:f\Rightarrow g$ and $\beta:g\Rightarrow h$ be 2-cells between 1-cells $A\to B$, and let $\alpha':f'\Rightarrow g'$ and $\beta':g'\Rightarrow h'$ be 2-cells between 1-cells $B\to C$. The interchange law says $(\beta'\ast\beta)\cdot(\alpha'\ast\alpha)=(\beta'\cdot\alpha')\ast(\beta\cdot\alpha)$, where $\cdot$ is [vertical composition](c:vertical-composition) and $\ast$ is [horizontal composition](c:horizontal-composition).
examples: In the 2-category of categories, functors and natural transformations, the interchange law holds for the composition of natural transformations.

In a [strict monoidal category](c:strict-monoidal-category), viewed as a 2-category with one object, the law says $(g\circ f)\otimes(g'\circ f')=(g\otimes g')\circ(f\otimes f')$, which is the functoriality of $\otimes$.
Eckmann-Hilton: two monoid structures on one set that satisfy the interchange law agree, and the common operation is commutative.
Non-example: the operations $+$ and $\cdot$ on $\mathbb Z$ do not satisfy $(a+b)\cdot(c+d)=(a\cdot c)+(b\cdot d)$, because $(1+1)\cdot(1+1)=4$ while $1\cdot1+1\cdot1=2$.

reminder: An intermediate field of an extension $L/K$ is a subfield of $L$ that contains $K$.
definition: Let $L/K$ be a [field extension](c:field-extension). An intermediate field is a [subfield](c:subfield) $E$ of $L$ with $K\subseteq E$, so that $K\subseteq E\subseteq L$ is a tower of field extensions. The intermediate fields of $L/K$ form a lattice under inclusion.
examples: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ is an intermediate field of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/\mathbb Q$.
The extension $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/\mathbb Q$ has exactly three intermediate fields strictly between $\mathbb Q$ and the top: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$ and $\mathbb Q(\sqrt6)$.
The extension $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ has only the two intermediate fields $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$, because its degree $2$ is prime.
Non-example: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$ is a subfield of $\mathbb R$, but it is not an intermediate field of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)/\mathbb Q$, because it is not contained in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$.

steps: Take an intermediate field $E$ of $L/K$.
By definition $E$ is a subset of $L$ that is closed under the field operations, so $E$ is a subfield of $L$.
The intermediate case adds the condition that $E$ contains $K$.
links.why: Facts about subfields of $L$ apply to every intermediate field.

reminder: An interval polynomial is a family of polynomials whose coefficients each range over a given closed interval.
definition: An interval polynomial is the set of all real [polynomials](c:polynomial) $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n$ with $a_i\in[\underline a_i,\overline a_i]$ for every $i$, where the $[\underline a_i,\overline a_i]$ are fixed closed [intervals](c:interval) of [real numbers](c:real-number). Kharitonov's theorem tests the stability of the whole family with four extreme members.
examples: The family $[1,2]+[0,3]x+x^2$ contains all polynomials $a_0+a_1x+x^2$ with $1\le a_0\le2$ and $0\le a_1\le3$.
Kharitonov's theorem: the family is Hurwitz stable exactly when its four extreme polynomials are.
Non-example: the set $\{a_0+a_1x:\ a_1=a_0^2,\ 0\le a_0\le1\}$ has coupled coefficients, so its coefficient set is a curve and not a box of intervals.

reminder: The intrinsic volumes of a convex body are the coefficients in the formula for the volume of its parallel bodies.
definition: For a [convex body](c:convex-body) $K$ in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb R^n$, the intrinsic volumes $V_0(K),\dots,V_n(K)$ are defined by the Steiner formula $\mathrm{vol}_n(K+tB^n)=\sum_{k=0}^n\omega_{n-k}t^{n-k}V_k(K)$ for $t\ge0$, where $B^n$ is the unit ball, $\omega_j$ is the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb R^j$ and $\mathrm{vol}_n$ is [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure). Then $V_n$ is the volume, $2V_{n-1}$ is the surface area and $V_0=1$.
examples: For the unit square in $\mathbb R^2$, $V_2=1$ is the area, $V_1=2$ is half the perimeter and $V_0=1$.
For the unit disc, $V_2=\pi$, $V_1=\pi$ and $V_0=1$.
Hadwiger's theorem: every continuous, motion-invariant valuation on convex bodies is a linear combination of the $V_k$.

Non-example: the diameter of a convex body is not an intrinsic volume, because it fails the valuation identity $\varphi(K\cup L)+\varphi(K\cap L)=\varphi(K)+\varphi(L)$ for convex $K,L$ with $K\cup L$ convex.

reminder: Intuitionistic logic accepts a statement only with a constructed proof, so it does not assume the law of excluded middle.
definition:
Intuitionistic logic is a logic with the connectives and quantifiers of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic) but only constructive rules for them. It does not prove the [law of excluded middle](c:law-of-excluded-middle) $P\lor
eg P$ or double-negation elimination $
eg
eg P	o P$, and a [proof](c:proof) of $P\lor Q$ must show which side holds, while a proof of $\exists x\,P(x)$ must give a witness.
examples: The formula $P\to\neg\neg P$ is provable in intuitionistic logic.
Every intuitionistically provable formula is classically valid; for example $(P\to Q)\to(\neg Q\to\neg P)$ is provable in both.
A proof of $\exists x\,P(x)$ in Heyting arithmetic yields a numeral $n$ with $P(n)$.

Non-example: $P\lor
eg P$ and $
eg
eg P	o P$ are classically valid, but intuitionistic logic does not prove them for an arbitrary statement $P$.

steps: Start with classical logic, which has all the rules of intuitionistic logic.
Classical logic also accepts the law of excluded middle $P\lor\neg P$ as an axiom scheme.
Dropping this one axiom scheme leaves intuitionistic logic, so every intuitionistic proof is a classical proof.
links.why: A theorem with an intuitionistic proof holds in classical logic and keeps a constructive meaning.

reminder: The irregularity of a smooth projective surface is the number $q=\dim H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$.
definition: The irregularity of a smooth projective [complex surface](c:complex-surface) $X$ is $q(X)=\dim H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$, the dimension of the first [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) group of its [structure sheaf](c:structure-sheaf). By Hodge theory it equals the dimension of the space of holomorphic $1$-forms on $X$, and $X$ is called regular when $q(X)=0$.
examples: The projective plane has $q=0$, and so has every rational surface.
An abelian surface such as $E\times E'$, with $E,E'$ elliptic curves, has $q=2$.
For $C\times\mathbb P^1$ with $C$ a curve of genus $g$, the irregularity is $q=g$.
Non-example: the geometric genus $p_g=\dim H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)$ is a different invariant; a K3 surface has $q=0$ but $p_g=1$.

reminder: Two elements of a bounded lattice are complements when their join is the top and their meet is the bottom.
definition: In a [lattice](c:lattice) with a least element $\bot$ and a greatest element $\top$ (a [bounded order](c:bounded-order)), two elements $x$ and $y$ are complements of each other when $x\sqcup y=\top$ and $x\sqcap y=\bot$. The relation is symmetric in $x$ and $y$.
examples: In the subsets of a set $S$ ordered by inclusion, $A$ and $S\setminus A$ are complements.
In the divisors of $6$ ordered by divisibility, $2$ and $3$ are complements, because their $\mathrm{lcm}$ is $6$ and their $\gcd$ is $1$.
Non-example: in the chain $0<\tfrac12<1$ the element $\tfrac12$ has no complement, because $\tfrac12\sqcup y=1$ forces $y=1$ and then $\tfrac12\sqcap1\ne0$.

reminder: A corner of a set $A\subseteq G\times G$ is a triple of points $(x,y)$, $(x+d,y)$, $(x,y+d)$ that all lie in $A$.
definition: Let $G$ be an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) and let $A$ be a [subset](c:subset) of the [product](c:cartesian-product) $G\times G$. A corner of $A$ is a triple of points $(x,y)$, $(x+d,y)$, $(x,y+d)$ that all lie in $A$, and it is nontrivial when $d\ne0$. A set with no nontrivial corner is corner-free.
examples: In $\mathbb Z^2$ the set $\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\}$ is itself a corner, with $x=y=0$ and $d=1$.
The grid $\{0,\dots,N-1\}^2$ contains many nontrivial corners, and the corners theorem says that every dense subset of a large grid contains one.
Non-example: the points $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)$ are not a corner, because taking $(1,0)$ as the corner point gives the steps $-1$ and $+1$, which are not equal.
The diagonal $\{(n,n):n\in\mathbb Z\}$ is corner-free, because $(x,y)$ and $(x+d,y)$ both on the diagonal force $d=0$.

reminder: A polynomial is distinguished at an ideal when it is monic and all its lower coefficients lie in the ideal.
definition: Let $I$ be an [ideal](c:ideal) of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$. A [polynomial](c:polynomial) $f\in R[X]$ of degree $n$ is distinguished at $I$ when $f$ is monic and every coefficient of $f$ below the leading one lies in $I$. Equivalently, $f-X^n$ has all its coefficients in $I$.
examples: $X^2+3X+6$ in $\mathbb Z[X]$ is distinguished at $I=(3)$, because it is monic and $3,6\in(3)$.
$X^n$ is distinguished at every ideal, because all its lower coefficients are $0$.
The Weierstrass preparation theorem writes a suitable power series as a unit times a polynomial distinguished at the maximal ideal.
Non-example: $X^2+X+3$ is monic, but at $I=(3)$ the coefficient $1$ of $X$ is not in $I$, so it is not distinguished.

steps: Take a polynomial $f$ that is distinguished at $I$.
By definition every coefficient of $f$ below the leading one lies in $I$, so $f$ is weakly Eisenstein at $I$.
The distinguished case adds the condition that $f$ is monic.
links.why: Facts about weakly Eisenstein polynomials apply to distinguished polynomials, which also have leading coefficient $1$.

reminder: A Grothendieck abelian category is an abelian category with exact filtered colimits and a separator.
definition: An [abelian category](c:abelian-category) $\mathcal C$ is Grothendieck abelian when it is locally small, has [filtered colimits](c:filtered-colimit) that are exact (axiom AB5), and has a [separator](c:has-separator), that is, an object $G$ such that any two different maps $A\to B$ differ after composing with some map $G\to A$.
examples: The category of modules over a ring $R$ is Grothendieck abelian, with $R$ as a separator.
The category of abelian groups and the category of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space are Grothendieck abelian.
Non-example: the category of finite abelian groups is abelian, but it lacks countable direct sums, which are filtered colimits of finite direct sums, so it has no exact filtered colimits.

steps: Take a Grothendieck abelian category $\mathcal C$.
By definition $\mathcal C$ is an abelian category.
The special case adds exact filtered colimits and a separator.
links.why: Every fact about abelian categories applies to a Grothendieck abelian category, which also has all colimits and enough injectives.

reminder: A Hahn decomposition of two measures is a measurable set where the first is smaller and whose complement reverses this.
definition:
Let $\mu$ and $
u$ be [measures](c:measure) on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space). A Hahn decomposition for $(\mu,
u)$ is a [measurable set](c:measurable-set) $s$ with $\mu(A)\le
u(A)$ for every measurable $A\subseteq s$ and $
u(A)\le\mu(A)$ for every measurable $A\subseteq s^c$. For finite measures one always exists, and it splits the [signed measure](c:signed-measure) $\mu-
u$ into a negative part on $s$ and a positive part on $s^c$.
examples: Let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$, $\mu=\lambda$ and $\nu(A)=2\lambda(A\cap[0,\tfrac12])$. Then $s=[0,\tfrac12]$ is a Hahn decomposition.
For $\mu=\delta_0$ and $\nu=\delta_1$ on $\mathbb R$, the set $s=\{1\}$ is a Hahn decomposition.
Non-example: $s=[0,1]$ fails in the first example, because for $A=(\tfrac12,1]$ we get $\mu(A)=\tfrac12>0=\nu(A)$.

reminder: A scheme is locally Noetherian when the ring of every affine open subset is Noetherian.
definition: A [scheme](c:scheme) $X$ is locally Noetherian if $\mathcal O_X(U)$ is a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring) for every [affine](c:affine-scheme) open set $U\subseteq X$. Equivalently, $X$ has an [open cover](c:open-cover) by affine open sets whose rings are Noetherian.
examples: $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ and the affine space $\mathbb A^n_k$ over a field $k$ are locally Noetherian.
Every scheme that is locally of finite type over a field is locally Noetherian.
An infinite disjoint union of copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is locally Noetherian, but it is not quasi-compact.
Non-example: $\operatorname{Spec}k[x_1,x_2,\dots]$ is not locally Noetherian, because a polynomial ring in infinitely many variables is not Noetherian.

steps: Take a Noetherian scheme $X$.
By definition $X$ is locally Noetherian and quasi-compact.
So $X$ is locally Noetherian, and the condition of quasi-compactness is dropped.
links.why: A local result for locally Noetherian schemes applies to every Noetherian scheme.

steps: Take a locally Noetherian scheme $X$.
By assumption $X$ is a scheme.
The special case adds that the ring of sections over every affine open set is Noetherian.
links.why: Facts about schemes apply to locally Noetherian schemes, which also have Noetherian local rings.

reminder: A Noetherian scheme is a locally Noetherian scheme that is also quasi-compact.
definition: A [scheme](c:scheme) $X$ is Noetherian when it is [locally Noetherian](c:is-locally-noetherian) and [quasi-compact](c:compact-space), that is, when $X$ is a finite union of affine open sets $\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ with every $A_i$ a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring).
examples: $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ and the projective space $\mathbb P^n_k$ over a field $k$ are Noetherian schemes.
Every scheme of finite type over a field or over $\mathbb Z$ is a Noetherian scheme.
Non-example: the disjoint union of infinitely many copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is locally Noetherian, but it is not quasi-compact, so it is not Noetherian.

steps: Take a Noetherian scheme $X$.
By definition $X$ is locally Noetherian, so each affine open set of $X$ has a Noetherian ring.
The Noetherian case adds that $X$ is quasi-compact, so finitely many affine open sets cover $X$.
links.why: Local statements about locally Noetherian schemes hold for Noetherian schemes, which also give finiteness results.

reminder: A von Neumann ordinal is a transitive set that the membership relation well-orders.
definition: A set $x$ is a von Neumann ordinal when it is transitive, meaning that $y\in x$ implies $y\subseteq x$, and the [membership relation](c:membership-relation) $\in$ is a strict [well order](c:well-order) on $x$. Every element of an ordinal is again an ordinal, and an ordinal is the set of all smaller ordinals.
examples: The sets $\varnothing$, $\{\varnothing\}$ and $\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\}\}$ are the ordinals $0$, $1$ and $2$.
The set $\omega$ of all finite ordinals is an ordinal, and so is $\omega\cup\{\omega\}$.
Non-example: $\{\{\varnothing\}\}$ is not an ordinal, because it is not transitive: its element $\{\varnothing\}$ is not a subset of it.

steps: Take a von Neumann ordinal $x$.
Then $(x,\in)$ is a well-ordered set, so it has an order type.
The set $x$ represents this order type, because $x$ is the set of all smaller ordinals.
The special case adds a canonical representative that is a set of sets.
links.why: Every ordinal number has exactly one von Neumann representative, so set-theoretic constructions can use sets as ordinals.

reminder: A primitive $k$-th root of unity $\zeta$ satisfies $\zeta^k=1$ and has no smaller positive power equal to $1$.
definition: Let $k\ge1$. An element $\zeta$ of a commutative [monoid](c:monoid), for example a field, is a primitive $k$-th [root of unity](c:root-of-unity) if $\zeta^k=1$ and every $l$ with $\zeta^l=1$ is divisible by $k$. Equivalently, $\zeta$ has multiplicative [order](c:order-of-an-element) exactly $k$.
examples: In $\mathbb C$ the number $e^{2\pi i/k}$ is a primitive $k$-th root of unity.
In the field $\mathbb F_7$ the element $3$ is a primitive $6$th root of unity, because its powers are $3,2,6,4,5,1$.
Non-example: $-1$ is a fourth root of unity but not a primitive one, because $(-1)^2=1$ and $4\nmid2$.

steps: Take a primitive $k$-th root of unity $\zeta$.
Then $\zeta^k=1$, so $\zeta$ is a $k$-th root of unity.
The primitive case adds that no smaller positive power of $\zeta$ equals $1$, so $\zeta$ has order exactly $k$.
links.why: Facts about roots of unity apply to primitive roots, which generate all $k$-th roots of unity in a field.

reminder: A quasi-coherent sheaf is a sheaf of modules that locally is the cokernel of a map between free modules.
definition: Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a [ringed space](c:ringed-space). A [sheaf of modules](c:module-sheaf) $\mathcal F$ on $X$ is quasi-coherent if every point has an open neighbourhood $U$ on which $\mathcal F$ is the [cokernel](c:cokernel) of a map $\bigoplus_{j\in J}\mathcal O_U\to\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathcal O_U$ between direct sums of copies of $\mathcal O_U$. On an affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}A$ these are exactly the sheaves $\widetilde M$ for $A$-modules $M$.
examples: The structure sheaf $\mathcal O_X$ and every sheaf $\widetilde M$ on $\operatorname{Spec}A$, for an $A$-module $M$, are quasi-coherent.
The ideal sheaf of a closed subscheme of a scheme $X$ is quasi-coherent.
Non-example: for $X=\mathbb A^1_k$ and $U=X\setminus\{0\}$, the extension by zero $j_!\mathcal O_U$ is not quasi-coherent, because its global sections are $0$ but the sheaf is not $0$.

steps: Take a quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal F$ on a ringed space $(X,\mathcal O_X)$.
By definition $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of $\mathcal O_X$-modules.
The special case adds a local presentation: near each point $\mathcal F$ is a cokernel of a map between free modules.
links.why: Facts about sheaves of modules apply to quasi-coherent sheaves, which also have a local description by modules.

steps: Take a coherent sheaf $\mathcal F$, which is locally finitely presented.
Near each point there is an exact sequence $\mathcal O^m\to\mathcal O^n\to\mathcal F\to0$.
Finite direct sums are special cases of the direct sums in the definition.
So $\mathcal F$ is quasi-coherent; the coherent case also forces $m$ and $n$ to be finite.
links.why: A result for quasi-coherent sheaves applies to every coherent sheaf.

reminder: A regular local ring is a Noetherian local ring whose maximal ideal needs as many generators as its Krull dimension.
definition: A [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring) [local ring](c:local-ring) $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ is regular if its [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak m$ is generated by $\dim R$ elements, where $\dim R$ is the [Krull dimension](c:krull-dimension). Equivalently, $\dim_k\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2=\dim R$, where $k=R/\mathfrak m$ is the [residue field](c:residue-field).
examples: A field is a regular local ring of dimension $0$.
The localization $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]_{(x_1,\dots,x_n)}$ is a regular local ring of dimension $n$.
Every discrete valuation ring, such as $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, is a regular local ring of dimension $1$.
Non-example: the cusp $k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3)$ localized at the origin has dimension $1$, but $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ has dimension $2$, so it is not regular.

steps: Take a regular local ring $R$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$.
By definition $R$ is a Noetherian local ring.
The regular case adds that $\mathfrak m$ is generated by $\dim R$ elements.
links.why: Facts about Noetherian local rings apply to regular local rings, which are also domains.

steps: Take a discrete valuation ring $R$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=(\pi)$.
Then $R$ is a Noetherian local ring of Krull dimension $1$.
The ideal $\mathfrak m$ is generated by the single element $\pi$, and $1=\dim R$, so $R$ is regular.
Regular local rings also allow every dimension $n$, with $n$ generators for $\mathfrak m$.
links.why: A result for regular local rings applies to every discrete valuation ring, the case of dimension one.

reminder: A functor $G$ is a right adjoint when maps $FX\to Y$ correspond naturally to maps $X\to GY$ for some functor $F$.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ is a right adjoint if some functor $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ has bijections between [hom-sets](c:hom-set), $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal D}(FX,Y)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,GY)$, that are natural in $X$ and $Y$. Then $F$ is a left adjoint of $G$, and $F$ and $G$ form an [adjoint functor](c:adjoint-functor) pair.
examples: The forgetful functor from groups to sets is a right adjoint, and its left adjoint builds the free group.
For a set $A$, the functor $Y\mapsto Y^A$ on sets is right adjoint to $X\mapsto X\times A$.
The inclusion of abelian groups into groups is a right adjoint, and its left adjoint is abelianization.

Non-example: the forgetful functor from fields to sets has no left adjoint, because a free field on one point would map to fields of every characteristic, but field homomorphisms preserve the characteristic.

reminder: A field extension is separable when every element has a minimal polynomial without repeated roots.
definition: A [field extension](c:field-extension) $K/F$ is separable if it is [algebraic](c:algebraic-extension) and the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) over $F$ of every element of $K$ is separable, that is, it has no repeated root in an algebraic closure. In characteristic $0$ every algebraic extension is separable.
examples: Every algebraic extension of a field of characteristic $0$, such as $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)/\mathbb Q$, is separable.
Every algebraic extension of a finite field, such as $\mathbb F_{p^n}/\mathbb F_p$, is separable.
Non-example: $\mathbb F_p(t)/\mathbb F_p(t^p)$ is not separable, because $t$ has the minimal polynomial $X^p-t^p=(X-t)^p$, which has a repeated root.

steps: Take a separable extension $K/F$.
Each element of $K$ has a minimal polynomial over $F$, so each element is algebraic.
So $K/F$ is an algebraic extension.
The separable case adds that every such minimal polynomial has distinct roots.
links.why: Facts about algebraic extensions apply to separable extensions, which also allow the primitive element theorem for finite ones.

steps: Take a Galois extension $K/F$, which is normal and separable by definition.
Dropping the normality condition leaves a separable extension.
So every Galois extension is separable.
The converse fails: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbb Q$ is separable but not normal.
links.why: A result for separable extensions applies to every Galois extension.

reminder: A morphism of schemes is separated when its diagonal map into the fibre product is a closed immersion.
definition: A [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) $f:X\to Y$ is separated if its [diagonal morphism](c:diagonal-morphism) $\Delta_f:X\to X\times_YX$ is a [closed immersion](c:is-closed-immersion). A scheme $X$ is separated when the morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ is separated.
examples: Every morphism between affine schemes is separated.
The projective line $\mathbb P^1_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is separated.
Non-example: the affine line with a doubled origin over a field $k$ is not separated, because the image of its diagonal is not closed.

steps: Take a separated morphism $f:X\to Y$.
By definition $f$ is a morphism of schemes.
The special case adds that the diagonal $X\to X\times_YX$ is a closed immersion.
links.why: Facts about morphisms of schemes apply to separated morphisms, which also have uniqueness of limits.

reminder: A smooth embedding is a smooth map that is an immersion and a homeomorphism onto its image.
definition: A [smooth map](c:smooth-map) $f:M\to M'$ between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) is a smooth embedding if it is an [immersion](c:immersion), so its differential is injective at every point, and a topological [embedding](c:embedding), so it is a homeomorphism onto its image with the subspace topology. Then $f(M)$ is an embedded submanifold of $M'$ that is diffeomorphic to $M$.
examples: The inclusion $S^n\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{n+1}$ of the sphere is a smooth embedding.
For a smooth function $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, the graph map $x\mapsto(x,g(x))$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R^2$ is a smooth embedding.
Non-example: $t\mapsto(t^2,t^3)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R^2$ is a topological embedding but not an immersion, because its derivative is $0$ at $t=0$.
Non-example: an injective immersion of an open interval onto a curve shaped like the digit 6, whose end approaches an inner point of the curve, is not a topological embedding.

steps: Take a smooth embedding $f:M\to M'$.
By definition $f$ is a smooth map with injective differential at every point.
So $f$ is an immersion.
The special case adds that $f$ is a homeomorphism onto its image.
links.why: Local facts about immersions apply to smooth embeddings, which also give submanifolds.

steps: Take a smooth embedding $f:M\to M'$.
By definition $f$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, so it is a topological embedding.
The smooth case adds that $f$ is smooth and that its differential is injective.
links.why: Facts about topological embeddings apply to smooth embeddings, which also keep the smooth structure.

reminder: A spanning subgraph of a graph $G$ is a subgraph with the same vertices as $G$.
definition: A [subgraph](c:is-subgraph) $H$ of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ is a spanning subgraph when $H$ has the same [vertex](c:vertex) set as $G$, so $H$ comes from $G$ by deleting edges only. In mathlib this relation is written $H\le_sG$.
examples: A spanning tree of a connected graph is a spanning subgraph of it.
A perfect matching of a graph is a spanning subgraph, because every vertex lies on one of its edges.
Non-example: the induced subgraph on a proper subset of the vertices is not spanning, because it misses a vertex.

steps: Take a spanning subgraph $H$ of $G$.
Its vertices are the vertices of $G$, and its edges are edges of $G$ with the same ends.
So $H$ is a subgraph of $G$.
The spanning case adds that $H$ keeps every vertex of $G$.
links.why: Facts about subgraphs apply to spanning subgraphs, which only delete edges.

steps: Take a spanning tree $T$ of a connected graph $G$.
The tree $T$ is a subgraph of $G$ that contains all vertices of $G$.
So $T$ is a spanning subgraph of $G$.
The spanning tree adds the condition that $T$ is connected and has no cycle.
links.why: A fact about spanning subgraphs applies to every spanning tree.

reminder: A subgraph of $G$ uses only vertices and edges of $G$, and each edge keeps its ends.
definition: A graph $H$ is a subgraph of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ when every [vertex](c:vertex) of $H$ is a vertex of $G$ and every [edge](c:edge) of $H$ is an edge of $G$ with the same ends. Then we write $H\subseteq G$.
examples: A single edge together with its two ends is a subgraph of a triangle.
Any cycle in $G$, taken with its vertices and edges, is a subgraph of $G$.
Non-example: the triangle $K_3$ is not a subgraph of the $4$-cycle $C_4$, because $C_4$ has no three vertices that are pairwise adjacent.

steps: Take a spanning subgraph $H$ of $G$.
Its vertices are the vertices of $G$, and its edges are edges of $G$.
So $H$ is a subgraph of $G$.
The spanning case adds that $H$ keeps every vertex of $G$.
links.why: A fact about subgraphs applies to spanning subgraphs, which only delete edges.

steps: Take a set $S$ of vertices of $G$ and the induced subgraph $G[S]$.
Its vertices lie in $S\subseteq V(G)$, and its edges are edges of $G$ with both ends in $S$.
So $G[S]$ is a subgraph of $G$.
The induced case adds that $G[S]$ keeps every edge of $G$ with both ends in $S$.
links.why: A fact about subgraphs applies to induced subgraphs, which keep all edges between their vertices.

reminder: An isogeny is a surjective homomorphism of algebraic groups with finite kernel.
definition: An isogeny is a [surjective](c:surjection) [homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) $\varphi:G\to H$ of [algebraic groups](c:algebraic-group) whose [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) is finite. For [abelian varieties](c:abelian-variety), a surjective homomorphism is an isogeny exactly when the two varieties have the same dimension.
examples: Multiplication by $n\ne0$ on an elliptic curve $E$ is an isogeny $E\to E$, with kernel $E[n]$.
The map $z\mapsto z^n$ on the multiplicative group $\mathbb G_m$ is an isogeny, with kernel the $n$-th roots of unity.
Non-example: the projection $E\times E\to E$ is surjective, but its kernel $\{0\}\times E$ is infinite, so it is not an isogeny.

steps: Take an isogeny $\varphi:G\to H$ of algebraic groups.
By definition $\varphi$ is a homomorphism of groups.
The special case adds that $\varphi$ is surjective with finite kernel.
links.why: Facts about group homomorphisms apply to isogenies, which also have a finite degree.

reminder: An isolated singularity is a singular point that has a neighbourhood with no other singular point.
definition: An isolated singularity of a [complex analytic space](c:complex-analytic-space) $X$ is a [singularity](c:singularity) $p$ of $X$ that has a neighbourhood containing no other singular point, so $X$ is smooth on a punctured neighbourhood of $p$. For a function $g$, the same word names a point where $g$ is not [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) although $g$ is holomorphic on a punctured disc around that point.
examples: The origin of the cone $x^2+y^2=z^2$ in $\mathbb C^3$ is an isolated singularity.
The origin of the cusp $y^2=x^3$ in $\mathbb C^2$ is an isolated singularity, because it is the only singular point.
The point $z=0$ is an isolated singularity of the function $1/z$.
Non-example: the origin of $xy=0$ in $\mathbb C^3$ is a singular point, but it is not isolated, because every point of the $z$-axis is singular.

steps: Take an isolated singularity $p$ of a space $X$.
By definition $p$ is a singular point of $X$, so it is a singularity.
The isolated case adds a neighbourhood of $p$ that contains no other singular point.
links.why: Facts about singularities apply to isolated singularities, which can also be studied through a punctured neighbourhood.

reminder: An isometric embedding is an embedding that keeps all distances between points, or for manifolds keeps the Riemannian metric.
definition: An isometric embedding of a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d_X)$ into $(Y,d_Y)$ is a map $f:X\to Y$ with $d_Y(f(x),f(x'))=d_X(x,x')$ for all $x,x'\in X$, and it is an [embedding](c:embedding) of spaces. For a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $(M,g)$ and a Riemannian manifold $(N,h)$, it is a smooth embedding $f:M\to N$ with $f^*h=g$.
examples: The map $x\mapsto(x,0)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R^2$ is an isometric embedding.
Every metric space has an isometric embedding into a space of bounded functions, by the Kuratowski embedding.
Nash embedding theorem: every Riemannian manifold has a smooth isometric embedding into some Euclidean space $\mathbb R^N$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto2x$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$ is an embedding but not an isometric one, because it doubles every distance.

steps: Take an isometric embedding $f:X\to Y$ of metric spaces.
It preserves distances, so $f$ is injective, because $f(x)=f(x')$ gives $d_X(x,x')=0$.
The inverse $f(X)\to X$ also preserves distances, so $f$ is a homeomorphism onto its image.
So $f$ is an embedding, and the isometric case adds that distances are kept exactly.
links.why: Facts about embeddings apply to isometric embeddings, which also keep every distance.

steps: Take an isometry $f:X\to Y$, that is, a distance-preserving bijection of metric spaces.
Since $f$ preserves distances, it is an isometric embedding.
An isometric embedding need not be surjective, for example $x\mapsto(x,0)$.
links.why: A result for isometric embeddings applies to every isometry.

reminder: The Jacobson radical of a ring is the intersection of all its maximal left ideals.
definition: For a [ring](c:ring) $R$ with $1$, the Jacobson radical $J(R)$ is the intersection of all [maximal](c:maximal-ideal) left ideals of $R$. Equivalently, $r\in J(R)$ exactly when $1-xr$ has a left inverse for every $x\in R$, and exactly when $r$ annihilates every [simple module](c:is-simple-module) over $R$.
examples: $J(\mathbb Z)=0$, because the intersection of all the ideals $(p)$ with $p$ prime is $0$.
For a [local ring](c:local-ring) $R$, $J(R)$ is the unique maximal ideal; for example $J(k[[t]])=(t)$.
$J(\mathbb Z/12)=(6)$, the intersection of the maximal ideals $(2)$ and $(3)$.
Non-example: $2\notin J(\mathbb Z/12)$, because $2$ does not lie in the maximal ideal $(3)$.

reminder: The joint distribution of random variables gives the probability that they take values in any given set together.
definition: For [random variables](c:random-variable) $X_1,\dots,X_n$ on one probability space, the joint distribution is the [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) of the vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$, that is, the measure $B\mapsto P((X_1,\dots,X_n)\in B)$ on $\mathbb R^n$. Its [marginal distributions](c:marginal-distribution) are the distributions of the single variables $X_i$.
examples: For two independent fair coin flips, each of the four outcomes has joint probability $\tfrac14$.
For the pair $(X,X)$, all the mass lies on the diagonal $\{(x,x)\}$ of $\mathbb R^2$.
A bivariate normal vector has a joint distribution that is given by a mean vector and a covariance matrix.
Non-example: the two marginal distributions alone are not the joint distribution; two independent fair coins and two equal fair coins have the same marginals but different joint distributions.

steps: Take random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ and the vector $X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)$.
The vector $X$ is a random variable with values in $\mathbb R^n$.
Its distribution is a probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$, so it is a probability distribution.
The special case adds that the distribution records several variables together.
links.why: Facts about probability distributions apply to joint distributions, which also have marginals.

reminder: A Jordan decomposition writes a finite signed measure as the difference of two mutually singular finite measures.
definition: A Jordan decomposition on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) is a pair $(\mu^+,\mu^-)$ of finite [measures](c:measure) that are mutually [singular](c:singular-measure), so some measurable set carries $\mu^+$ and its complement carries $\mu^-$. It represents the [signed measure](c:signed-measure) $\mu^+-\mu^-$, and every finite signed measure has exactly one such pair.
examples:
For $
u(A)=\int_Ax\,dx$ on $[-1,1]$, the parts are $
u^+(A)=\int_{A\cap[0,1]}x\,dx$ and $
u^-(A)=\int_{A\cap[-1,0]}(-x)\,dx$.
For $\nu=\delta_0-\delta_1$, the Jordan decomposition is the pair $(\delta_0,\delta_1)$.
Non-example: for $\nu=\lambda$ on $[0,1]$ the pair $(2\lambda,\lambda)$ has difference $\nu$, but its two measures are not mutually singular; the Jordan decomposition is $(\lambda,0)$.

reminder: A K-orientation of a vector bundle is a Thom class in K-theory that generates the K-theory of each fibre sphere.
definition: A K-orientation of a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $V\to X$ of rank $n$ is a Thom class for [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory): a class $u$ in the K-theory of the [Thom space](c:thom-space) of $V$ whose restriction to each fibre sphere $S^n$ generates the K-theory of $S^n$ over the K-theory of a point. It is the case $E=K$ of an [orientation in generalized cohomology](c:orientation-in-generalized-cohomology).
examples: Every complex vector bundle has a K-orientation, which the Bott class built from the Koszul complex gives.
A real vector bundle with a spin$^c$ structure has a K-orientation, by the construction of Atiyah, Bott and Shapiro.
Non-example: the Möbius line bundle over $S^1$ has the Thom space $\mathbb{RP}^2$, and $\tilde K^1(\mathbb{RP}^2)=0$, so it has no Thom class and no K-orientation.

steps: Take a generalized cohomology theory $E$ and a vector bundle $V$ of rank $n$.
An $E$-orientation of $V$ is a class in $E^n$ of the Thom space that restricts to a generator on each fibre.
Choose $E$ to be topological K-theory.
Then an $E$-orientation is exactly a K-orientation.
links.why: Results on orientations in generalized cohomology, such as Thom isomorphisms, apply to K-orientations.

reminder: A Kac-Moody algebra is the Lie algebra that a generalized Cartan matrix defines by generators and relations.
definition: Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be a generalized Cartan [matrix](c:matrix), that is, $a_{ii}=2$, $a_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and $a_{ij}=0$ exactly when $a_{ji}=0$. The Kac-Moody algebra $\mathfrak g(A)$ is the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over $\mathbb C$ generated by elements $e_i,f_i$ and a [Cartan subalgebra](c:cartan-subalgebra) $\mathfrak h$ with $[e_i,f_j]=\delta_{ij}h_i$, $[h,e_i]=\alpha_i(h)e_i$, $[h,f_i]=-\alpha_i(h)f_i$ and $\alpha_j(h_i)=a_{ij}$, taken modulo the largest ideal that meets $\mathfrak h$ only in $0$.
examples: A Cartan matrix of finite type gives a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra, such as $\mathfrak{sl}_n$.
The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$ gives the affine Kac-Moody algebra of type $A_1^{(1)}$, which is infinite-dimensional.
Non-example: the Heisenberg Lie algebra is not a Kac-Moody algebra, because a nonzero Kac-Moody algebra contains copies of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ and is not nilpotent.

steps: Take a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak s$ with Cartan matrix $A$ of finite type.
Serre's theorem presents $\mathfrak s$ by generators $e_i,f_i,h_i$ with the relations of the Kac-Moody construction.
So $\mathfrak s$ is the Kac-Moody algebra $\mathfrak g(A)$ of a matrix of finite type.
A generalized Cartan matrix of infinite type gives an infinite-dimensional algebra instead.
links.why: Results for Kac-Moody algebras apply to every semisimple Lie algebra, the case of finite type.

reminder: The module of Kähler differentials of $B$ over $A$ is the universal target for $A$-derivations of $B$.
definition: For a commutative ring $A$ and an $A$-[algebra](c:algebra) $B$, the Kähler differentials form a $B$-[module](c:module) $\Omega_{B/A}$ with an $A$-[derivation](c:derivation) $d:B\to\Omega_{B/A}$ that has the [universal property](c:universal-property): every $A$-derivation $D:B\to M$ into a $B$-module $M$ factors uniquely as $D=\varphi\circ d$ with $\varphi$ a $B$-linear map. The module is generated by the symbols $db$ for $b\in B$, with $d(bb')=b\,db'+b'\,db$.
examples: For $B=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over $k$, the module $\Omega_{B/k}$ is the free $B$-module on $dx_1,\dots,dx_n$.
If $B=A/I$, or $B$ is a localization of $A$, then $\Omega_{B/A}=0$.
Non-example: the free $B$-module $B\,dx$ is not $\Omega_{B/k}$ for $B=k[x]/(x^2)$ when $2$ is invertible, because $d(x^2)=2x\,dx$ must be $0$, which makes $\Omega_{B/k}$ one-dimensional over $k$.

steps: Take a ring map $A\to B$ and its cotangent complex $L_{B/A}$.
The degree-$0$ homology $H_0(L_{B/A})$ is the module $\Omega_{B/A}$ of Kähler differentials.
For a smooth map $A\to B$, the complex $L_{B/A}$ is $\Omega_{B/A}$ in degree $0$.
links.why: Statements about the cotangent complex give back the Kähler differentials as its lowest part.

reminder: The KdV hierarchy is an infinite family of commuting flows that begins with the Korteweg-de Vries equation.
definition: The KdV hierarchy is the infinite sequence of commuting evolution [partial differential equations](c:partial-differential-equation) $\partial_{t_n}L=[P_n,L]$ for the operator $L=\partial_x^2+u(x)$, where $P_n$ is the [differential operator](c:differential-operator) of order $2n+1$ that is the differential part of $L^{n+1/2}$. The flow for $n=1$ is a form of the Korteweg-de Vries equation, $u_t=\tfrac14u_{xxx}+\tfrac32uu_x$.
examples: The flow for $n=0$ is $u_t=u_x$, a translation, and the flow for $n=1$ is the KdV equation, whose solutions include solitons.
The generating function of intersection numbers on moduli spaces of curves satisfies the KdV hierarchy, which is Witten's conjecture.
Non-example: Burgers' equation $u_t=u_{xx}+2uu_x$ is not in the hierarchy, because every flow of the hierarchy has odd order in $x$.

steps: Take the KdV hierarchy $\partial_{t_n}L=[P_n,L]$ for $L=\partial_x^2+u$.
These flows commute, and they have infinitely many conserved quantities such as $\int u\,dx$ and $\int u^2\,dx$.
So the hierarchy is an integrable system with infinitely many degrees of freedom.
The special case adds the explicit Lax form with the operator $L$.
links.why: General results on integrable systems apply to the KdV hierarchy, the standard example with infinitely many degrees of freedom.

reminder: The Kirby-Siebenmann invariant of a topological manifold is the class in $H^4(M;\mathbb Z/2)$ that obstructs a PL structure.
definition: The Kirby-Siebenmann invariant of a topological [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ is a class $\mathrm{ks}(M)\in H^4(M;\mathbb Z/2)$ in [cohomology](c:cohomology) that is the obstruction to lifting the stable [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle) of $M$ from a topological structure to a PL structure. In dimension at least $5$, $\mathrm{ks}(M)=0$ exactly when $M$ has a [piecewise-linear](c:piecewise-linear-manifold) structure.
examples: Every smooth or PL manifold has $\mathrm{ks}=0$.
The $E_8$ manifold, a closed simply connected topological $4$-manifold with intersection form $E_8$, has $\mathrm{ks}=1$, so it has no PL structure.
Non-example: $\mathrm{ks}$ does not decide whether a PL manifold has a smooth structure, because $\mathrm{ks}$ vanishes on every PL manifold, including PL manifolds without a smooth structure.

reminder: KK-theory assigns to two C*-algebras $A$ and $B$ an abelian group $KK(A,B)$ that generalizes both K-theory and K-homology.
definition: For separable [C*-algebras](c:c-star-algebra) $A$ and $B$, the group $KK(A,B)$ is the set of [homotopy](c:homotopy) classes of Kasparov $(A,B)$-modules $(E,\phi,F)$, with the sum given by direct sum. Here $E$ is a graded [Hilbert C*-module](c:c-star-module) over $B$, $\phi:A\to\mathcal L(E)$ is a graded $*$-homomorphism, and $F$ is an odd operator on $E$ such that $[F,\phi(a)]$, $(F^2-1)\phi(a)$ and $(F-F^*)\phi(a)$ are [compact](c:compact-operator) for all $a\in A$.
examples: $KK(\mathbb C,B)$ is the operator K-theory group $K_0(B)$.
$KK(A,\mathbb C)$ is the K-homology group $K^0(A)$.
The Kasparov product $KK(A,B)\times KK(B,C)\to KK(A,C)$ composes classes, and the class of an elliptic operator on $M$ lies in $KK(C(M),\mathbb C)$.
Non-example: the triple $(L^2(S^1),\text{multiplication},F=0)$ is not a Kasparov $(C(S^1),\mathbb C)$-module, because $(F^2-1)\phi(a)=-\phi(a)$ is not compact.

steps: Take a $C^*$-algebra $B$ and the algebra $A=\mathbb C$.
A Kasparov $(\mathbb C,B)$-module is a graded Hilbert $B$-module with an odd operator that is invertible modulo compact operators.
Its class is an element of the operator K-theory group $K_0(B)$, and this gives $KK(\mathbb C,B)\cong K_0(B)$.
links.why: A result for KK-theory applies to operator K-theory, the case where the first algebra is the complex numbers.

steps: Take a separable $C^*$-algebra $A$ and the algebra $B=\mathbb C$.
A Kasparov $(A,\mathbb C)$-module is a Fredholm module over $A$: a representation of $A$ on a Hilbert space with an operator $F$.
Classes of Fredholm modules form the K-homology group, so $KK(A,\mathbb C)\cong K^0(A)$.
links.why: A result for KK-theory applies to K-homology, the case where the second algebra is the complex numbers.

reminder: The Kleene star $L^*$ of a language $L$ is the set of all finite concatenations of words of $L$, including the empty word.
definition: For a set $L$ of words over an alphabet, that is, a [formal language](c:language), the Kleene star is $L^*=\bigcup_{n\ge0}L^n$, where $L^0=\{\varepsilon\}$ contains only the empty [word](c:word) and $L^{n+1}=\{uv:u\in L^n,\ v\in L\}$ is built by concatenation. So $L^*$ is the set of all finite concatenations of words of $L$.
examples: $\{a\}^*=\{\varepsilon,a,aa,aaa,\dots\}$.
$\{ab,c\}^*$ contains $\varepsilon$, $ab$, $c$, $abc$, $cab$, $abab$ and so on.
$\varnothing^*=\{\varepsilon\}$ and $\{\varepsilon\}^*=\{\varepsilon\}$.
Non-example: the word $ba$ is not in $\{ab\}^*$, because every element of $\{ab\}^*$ is a string of copies of $ab$.

steps: Take a set $\Sigma$ and view it as the language of one-letter words.
Its Kleene star $\Sigma^*$ is the set of all finite words over $\Sigma$.
With concatenation and the empty word, $\Sigma^*$ is the free monoid on $\Sigma$.
A general language $L$ gives only the submonoid of $\Sigma^*$ that $L$ generates.
links.why: Facts about the free monoid on an alphabet are the special case $L=\Sigma$ of facts about Kleene stars.

reminder: The Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equation is a system of differential equations whose operators form a flat connection on the configuration space of points in the plane.
definition: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) with a nondegenerate invariant symmetric bilinear form, let $\Omega\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$ be its Casimir tensor, and let $V_1,\dots,V_N$ be [representations](c:lie-algebra-representation) of $\mathfrak g$. The KZ equation for a function $\Psi(z_1,\dots,z_N)$ with values in $V_1\otimes\cdots\otimes V_N$ is $\partial_{z_i}\Psi=\hbar\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{\Omega_{ij}}{z_i-z_j}\Psi$ for $i=1,\dots,N$, where $\Omega_{ij}$ acts as $\Omega$ on the factors $i$ and $j$. The operators on the right form a [flat connection](c:flat-connection) on the [configuration space](c:configuration-space) of $N$ distinct points in $\mathbb C$.
examples: For $N=2$ the equation reduces to $\partial_{z_1}\Psi=\hbar\,\Omega\Psi/(z_1-z_2)$, with the solutions $(z_1-z_2)^{\hbar\Omega}v$.
For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$ the solutions are given by hypergeometric integrals.
The monodromy of the equation gives a representation of the braid group, which the Drinfeld-Kohno theorem identifies with the one from a quantum group.
Non-example: the two-dimensional nonabelian Lie algebra has no nondegenerate invariant form, so it has no Casimir tensor and no KZ equation.

reminder: The Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy of a measure-preserving map is the largest long-run growth rate of the entropy of partitions refined by the map.
definition: Let $T$ be a [measure-preserving map](c:measure-preserving-map) of a space $X$ with [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu$. For a finite [partition](c:finpartition) $P$ of $X$ into measurable sets, $h(T,P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1nH(P\vee T^{-1}P\vee\dots\vee T^{-(n-1)}P)$, where $H(Q)=-\sum_{A\in Q}\mu(A)\log\mu(A)$ is the [entropy](c:entropy) of $Q$. The Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is $h(T)=\sup_Ph(T,P)$ over all finite measurable partitions $P$.
examples: The identity map and every irrational rotation of the circle have entropy $0$.
The doubling map $x\mapsto2x\bmod1$ with Lebesgue measure has entropy $\log2$.
A Bernoulli shift with probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_k$ has entropy $-\sum p_i\log p_i$.
Non-example: for the doubling map the trivial partition $P=\{X\}$ gives $h(T,P)=0$, which is not $h(T)=\log2$; only a generating partition gives the full entropy.

reminder: A Koszul algebra is a graded algebra whose ground field has a projective resolution with $i$th term generated in degree $i$.
definition: Let $A=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}A_i$ be a positively [graded algebra](c:graded-algebra) over a field $k$ with $A_0=k$. Then $A$ is Koszul if the trivial module $k=A/A_{\ge1}$ has a graded [projective resolution](c:has-projective-resolution) $\cdots\to P_2\to P_1\to P_0\to k$ in which each $P_i$ is generated in degree $i$. Equivalently, the internal and homological gradings of $\mathrm{Ext}_A(k,k)$ agree; see [Ext](c:ext).
examples: The polynomial algebra $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is Koszul, with the Koszul complex as the resolution of $k$.
The exterior algebra $\Lambda(V)$ and the tensor algebra $T(V)$ are Koszul.
Non-example: $k[x]/(x^3)$ is not Koszul, because the second term of the resolution of $k$ is generated in degree $3$, not in degree $2$.

steps: Take a Koszul algebra $A$.
By definition $A$ is a positively graded algebra with $A_0=k$.
The Koszul case adds the condition that the resolution of $k$ is linear.
links.why: Facts about graded algebras apply to Koszul algebras, which also have a Koszul dual.

steps: Take a Koszul algebra $A$ with $A_0=k$.
In the resolution of $k$ the term $P_1$ is generated in degree $1$, so $A$ is generated by $A_1$.
The term $P_2$ is generated in degree $2$, so all relations of $A$ lie in degree $2$.
So $A$ is a quadratic algebra, and the Koszul case adds that the whole resolution is linear.
links.why: Facts about quadratic algebras apply to Koszul algebras, which are the quadratic algebras with a linear resolution.

reminder: The Kullback-Leibler divergence of $P$ from $Q$ is the expectation under $P$ of $\log(P/Q)$.
definition: For [probability distributions](c:probability-distribution) $P$ and $Q$ on a finite set, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\sum_xP(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$ with $0\log0=0$, and the value is $+\infty$ when $Q(x)=0<P(x)$ for some $x$. In general it equals $\int\log\frac{dP}{dQ}\,dP$, using the [Radon-Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) $dP/dQ$, when $P$ is [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure) with respect to $Q$, and it is $+\infty$ otherwise.
examples: $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|P)=0$ for every distribution $P$.
For $P=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and $Q=(\tfrac14,\tfrac34)$, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\tfrac12\log\tfrac43\approx0.144$ in nats.
Gibbs' inequality says that $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\ge0$, with equality only when $P=Q$.
Non-example: it is not a metric, because it is not symmetric; for the same $P$ and $Q$, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)\approx0.131$ differs from $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\approx0.144$.

steps: Take the convex function $f(t)=t\log t$ with $f(1)=0$.
The $f$-divergence is $D_f(P\|Q)=\int f\!\left(\frac{dP}{dQ}\right)dQ$ for $P$ absolutely continuous with respect to $Q$.
For this $f$ it equals $\int\frac{dP}{dQ}\log\frac{dP}{dQ}\,dQ=\int\log\frac{dP}{dQ}\,dP$.
So the Kullback-Leibler divergence is the $f$-divergence for $f(t)=t\log t$.
links.why: Facts about $f$-divergences, such as non-negativity and monotonicity under processing, apply to the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

reminder: The L-genus of a closed oriented $4k$-manifold is a polynomial in its Pontryagin classes, and it equals the signature.
definition: The L-genus assigns to a closed oriented [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ of dimension $4k$ the number $L(M)=\langle L_k(p_1,\dots,p_k),[M]\rangle$, where the $p_i$ are the [Pontryagin classes](c:pontryagin-class) of $M$ and $L_k$ is the degree-$k$ part of the multiplicative sequence of the [power series](c:power-series) $\sqrt z/\tanh\sqrt z$. By Hirzebruch's signature theorem, $L(M)$ equals the [signature](c:signature) of $M$.
examples: Since $L_1=p_1/3$ and $p_1(\mathbb{CP}^2)=3x^2$, we get $L(\mathbb{CP}^2)=1=\sigma(\mathbb{CP}^2)$.
Since $L_2=(7p_2-p_1^2)/45$, the L-genus of $\mathbb{CP}^4$ is $(70-25)/45=1$.
Non-example: the [Â-genus](c:a-hat-genus) uses the series $\frac{\sqrt z/2}{\sinh(\sqrt z/2)}$ and is not the L-genus; it gives $-\tfrac18$ for $\mathbb{CP}^2$, while $L(\mathbb{CP}^2)=1$.

reminder: The Langlands dual group of a reductive group $G$ has the dual root datum, so characters swap with cocharacters and roots with coroots.
definition: Let $G$ be a connected [reductive group](c:reductive-group) with [maximal torus](c:maximal-torus) $T$. Its Langlands dual group $\hat G$ is the complex connected reductive group whose root datum is dual to that of $G$: the characters and cocharacters of $T$ swap roles, and so do the roots and coroots. In the number-theoretic setting, the L-group ${}^LG$ is the semidirect product of $\hat G$ with a Galois group.
examples: $GL_n$ is self-dual: $\widehat{GL_n}=GL_n(\mathbb C)$.
$\widehat{SL_n}=PGL_n(\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat{PGL_n}=SL_n(\mathbb C)$.
$\widehat{SO_{2n+1}}=Sp_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat{Sp_{2n}}=SO_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$.
Non-example: $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is not the dual group of $SL_2$; the dual group of $SL_2$ is $PGL_2(\mathbb C)$.

reminder: A formal language is a set of finite strings of symbols taken from a fixed alphabet.
definition: A formal language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ is a set of [words](c:word), that is, finite strings of symbols from $\Sigma$, usually picked out by rules such as a grammar. In [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic), a language instead fixes the function symbols and relation symbols, each with an arity, and these determine which strings are terms and formulas.
examples: The set of binary strings with an even number of $1$s is a formal language over $\{0,1\}$.
The set of well-formed arithmetic expressions, such as $(2+3)\cdot4$, is a formal language over digits, operators and brackets.
The first-order language of groups has a constant $1$, a binary function symbol $\cdot$ and a unary function symbol $^{-1}$.
Non-example: a set of infinite sequences such as $0101\dots$ is not a formal language, because words must be finite.

steps: Take a regular language $R$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, that is, a set of words that a finite automaton recognizes.
Each element of $R$ is a finite word over $\Sigma$.
So $R$ is a set of words over $\Sigma$, which is a formal language.
The regular case adds that a finite automaton recognizes the set.
links.why: A fact about formal languages applies to every regular language.

reminder: A lattice is a partially ordered set in which every two elements have a join and a meet.
definition: A lattice is a [partial order](c:partial-order) $(L,\le)$ in which every two elements $x,y$ have a [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) $x\vee y$, the join, and a greatest lower bound $x\wedge y$, the [meet](c:meet). Equivalently, a lattice is a set with two commutative, associative operations $\vee,\wedge$ that satisfy the absorption laws $x\vee(x\wedge y)=x$ and $x\wedge(x\vee y)=x$.
examples: Every totally ordered set, such as $(\mathbb R,\le)$, is a lattice with $x\vee y=\max(x,y)$ and $x\wedge y=\min(x,y)$.
The subsets of a set, ordered by inclusion, form a lattice with union as join and intersection as meet.
The positive integers ordered by divisibility form a lattice with $\mathrm{lcm}$ as join and $\gcd$ as meet.
Non-example: in the poset $\{a,b,c,d\}$ with $a,b<c$ and $a,b<d$, the elements $a$ and $b$ have the two upper bounds $c$ and $d$ but no least upper bound.

steps: Take a lattice $(L,\le)$.
By definition $\le$ is a partial order on $L$.
The lattice case adds a join and a meet for every pair of elements.
links.why: Order-theoretic facts about posets apply to every lattice.

steps: Take a distributive lattice $L$.
By definition $L$ is a lattice, so any two elements have a join and a meet.
The distributive case adds the law $x\wedge(y\vee z)=(x\wedge y)\vee(x\wedge z)$.
links.why: A result for lattices applies to every distributive lattice.

steps: Take a complete lattice $L$, where every subset has a supremum and an infimum.
For $x,y\in L$ the subset $\{x,y\}$ has the supremum $x\vee y$ and the infimum $x\wedge y$.
So $L$ is a lattice.
The complete case adds suprema and infima of infinite subsets.
links.why: A result for lattices applies to every complete lattice.

reminder: A lattice point is a point whose coordinates are all integers.
definition: A lattice point in $\mathbb R^n$ is a point $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ such that every coordinate $x_i$ is an [integer](c:integer). The lattice points form the integer lattice $\mathbb Z^n$ inside [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space).
examples: The point $(3,-2)$ and the origin $(0,0)$ are lattice points of the plane.
Pick's theorem computes the area of a polygon with lattice-point vertices from the lattice points on it and inside it.
Non-example: $(\tfrac12,1)$ is not a lattice point, because $\tfrac12$ is not an integer.

reminder: A Lawvere theory is a category with finite products in which every object is a finite power of one object.
definition: A Lawvere theory is a [category](c:category) $T$ with [finite products](c:has-finite-products) whose objects are the finite powers $\theta^n$, for $n\ge0$, of one object $\theta$, with $\theta^0$ the [terminal object](c:terminal-object). A model of $T$ is a functor $T\to\mathbf{Set}$ that preserves finite products.
examples: In the Lawvere theory of groups, the morphisms $\theta^n\to\theta$ are the $n$-ary operations that the group axioms allow, such as $(x,y)\mapsto xy^{-1}$.
The theories of monoids and of commutative rings are Lawvere theories whose models are monoids and commutative rings.
The opposite of the category of finite sets is the Lawvere theory of sets, which has no operations except projections.
Non-example: $\mathbf{Set}$ has finite products, but its objects are not all powers of one object, so it is not a Lawvere theory.

steps: Take a Lawvere theory $T$.
By definition $T$ is a category with finite products.
The special case adds that every object is a finite power of one object $\theta$.
links.why: Facts about categories with finite products apply to Lawvere theories, which also present algebraic theories.
